definition: In linguistics, center embedding is the process of embedding a phrase in the middle of another phrase of the same type.
details: This often leads to difficulty with parsing which would be difficult to explain on grammatical grounds alone. The most frequently used example involves embedding a relative clause inside another one as in: A man that a woman loves ⇒ {\displaystyle \Rightarrow } A man that a woman that a child knows loves ⇒ {\displaystyle \Rightarrow } A man that a woman that a child that a bird saw knows loves ⇒ {\displaystyle \Rightarrow } A man that a woman that a child that a bird that I heard saw knows loves In theories of natural language parsing, the difficulty with multiple center embedding is thought to arise from limitations of the human short term memory. In order to process multiple center embeddings, we have to store many subjects in order to connect them to their predicates. An interesting theoretical point is that sentences with multiple center embedding are grammatical, but unacceptable. Such examples are behind Noam Chomsky's comment that, "Languages are not 'designed for parsability' ... we may say that languages, as such, are not usable." explainer.lead: Center embedding happens when a phrase is interrupted by another phrase of the same kind, creating a sentence within a sentence. It matters because repeated nesting can remain grammatical while becoming very difficult for people to understand.

tiers.eli5: Imagine starting to describe a man, then pausing to describe a woman, then pausing again to describe a child. You have to remember all the unfinished parts before you can return to them and finish the sentence. After a few layers, your memory can struggle even though the sentence still follows the grammar.
tiers.practitioner: In parsing and grammar work, center embedding is a stress case for relating several pending subjects to predicates that arrive later. The classic relative-clause examples help distinguish grammaticality from acceptability and processing difficulty. A parsing failure alone does not establish a grammatical problem; the proposed human limitation is the short-term memory needed to keep track of the nested material.
tiers.paperLevel: Center embedding inserts a phrase into the middle of another phrase of the same type; repeated embedding of relative clauses yields forms such as "A man that a woman that a child knows loves." The proposed processing account requires maintaining several subjects until their predicates arrive, making difficulty increase under short-term-memory limitations. Multiple center embeddings can therefore be grammatical yet unacceptable, a distinction behind Noam Chomsky's remark that languages are not "designed for parsability."

explainer.example: In "A man that a woman that a child knows loves," the clause "that a child knows" is embedded inside "that a woman loves." The child does the knowing and the woman does the loving; holding those relationships open while completing the nested clauses illustrates the processing burden.

explainer.intuition: Center embedding tucks a phrase into the middle of another phrase of the same kind. One layer can be manageable, but repeated nesting leaves several sentence openings waiting for their endings.
howItWorks: Start with a phrase containing a relative clause: "A man that a woman loves."
Insert another relative clause inside it: "A man that a woman that a child knows loves."
Keep track of the subjects while waiting to connect them with their predicates.
Add further embeddings and the memory burden grows, making the sentence increasingly difficult to parse.
explainer.whyItMatters: It shows why a sentence can be grammatically valid yet unacceptable to human readers or listeners. It also gives theories of natural-language parsing a concrete case for studying memory limitations rather than treating every difficulty as a failure of grammar.
misconceptions: Multiple center embedding is not automatically ungrammatical; it can be grammatical yet unacceptable.
It is not merely making a sentence longer: the distinctive feature is nesting material inside an unfinished phrase of the same type.

diagram.caption: Each clause opens before the previous structure has been completed, producing nested material that the reader must keep track of.
